pr_title: Fix a memory order issue with weakly ordered systems (yet another alternative)
pr_body:
this adds a dummy atomic release operation to update_qp, which should make sure that the new value of reader_idx is visible in get_hold_current_qp, directly after incrementing the users count.

Fixes: #26875
pr_comments:
@davidben what do you think about this alternative?
In my previous testing this had also worked. But I did not see any reason to prefer this over other variants.
However in the light of the specification you mentioned, which says
"This promise only holds if B actually returns the value that A stored, or a value from later in the release sequence"
this might now make more sense.
This pull request is ready to merge
@bernd-edlinger @nhorman Should we just merge this to try if any failure reappears?
I would wait and test first we still have #26961 as a last resort.

linux-arm64 test is currently at 2377 iterations with no failures. If we're ok with waiting until post alpha (which I think we could be ok with, given this is a bug), we can wait until friday to merge, which would give us a 48 hour runway of testing, which would be good since #26962 failed after 10000 iterations.
4735 iterations on the arm64 test, still no failures, will leave it running overnight
Can you also take care of macos M1 testing, please?

I will, but I just hit an error in the linux-arm64 test on the code for this PR:

running at commit 7005e396d1ec5d8bf475473c6e4cd249b442eb62

i should note here that I'm specifically testing the branch from this PR, which has neither the debug asserts you previously had in place, nor does it incorporate the delayed retirement that we recently  merged.  You were asking about the debug output from some of that previously, and that would explain why its not present.  So far in my testing the only thing that has prevented failures has been the delayed retirement.
That is okay, the delayed retirement makes only a difference in the new test case that was added in the same PR.

I would now fall back to #26961 at commit df7c6b3d624c573b03cd32edb0df49f6eba34820
so that the results are exactly comparable.

Well, I am not really surprised that this did not work either.

If I would design a system that takes advantage of such a subtle detail of the C11 atomic spec,
that would for sure require a very complicated memory bus protocol, and in that case I would
definitely say at least a few words about that invention in the processor's assembler specification.

But I think this part of the C11 atomic specification is currently a purely theoretic issue where nobody
knows, how to implement it properly, and it reminds me a lot to the well known strict aliasing rules,
which were initially also a purely theoretic possibility for compiler optimizations, but when the
compilers actually started to implement those rules that caused lots of damage.

Note: Ran this same branch on an mac m1, and am at 14957 iterations running overnight with no failures.  This does seem to suggest that this patch works, but may be encountering a compiler issue on linux-arm64, or something simmilar.
@nhorman does the corrected test case work in your testing?

trying now

btw, also ran a test on the master branch with this change:
```
--- a/crypto/threads_pthread.c
+++ b/crypto/threads_pthread.c
@@ -281,7 +281,7 @@ static struct rcu_qp *get_hold_current_qp(struct rcu_lock_st *lock)
 
         /* if the idx hasn't changed, we're good, else try again */
         if (qp_idx == ATOMIC_LOAD_N(uint32_t, &lock->reader_idx,
-                                    __ATOMIC_RELAXED))
+                                    __ATOMIC_ACQUIRE))
             break;
```
ran overnight, 20222 on arm64, no failures

The test4.c and test5.c I cannot test here, but they clearly need similar changes.
But at least the assembler statement should be changed to tell the compiler that this
assembler instruction affects the memory, so it needs to be written as:
`asm volatile ("dmb sy":::"memory");`

> ran overnight, 20222 on arm64, no failures

Nice, but on macos this fails miserably:
https://github.com/bernd-edlinger/openssl/actions/runs/13722166308/job/38379923447
BTW, how it your macos test loop doing with this PR?
I ended [this test](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26964#issuecomment-2703763707) a few hours after I wrote that comment, no failures encountered.

Since there was a bit of confusion recently,
can we please double-check that this PR does *not* work on linux-arm64 and/or macos M1?
restarting tests for this branch on both platforms
this PR ran on both mac m1 and linux-arm64 overnight no failures, letting them continue for another day
closing in favor of #27002
So the test result was?
sorry, forgot to update this, ran for 48 hours on both arm64 and mac m1, no failures on either platform

But what if the original test failure https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26964#issuecomment-2701958335 was by mistake e.g. accidentally running #26982 instead of this PR?
In that case this would be preferable over #27002 wouldn't it?

And on the other hand, if we can prove that this PR failed twice on yoiur machine, this would be a definitive proof
of a hardware fault in the AARCH64 platform.  So definitely worth the effort to continue the testing for another weekend...

there are too many PR's floating about to test with here, this is getting too confusing.  I will run this PR #26964 for another weekend on both platforms and report on monday.  But we know that #27002 and #27012 work, so, barring negative results here, I would like to move forward with those.
Thanks, either way this result well be valuable.
both platforms still running well, will keep them going over the weekend.

fyi, I found errata 1946160 here:
https://developer.arm.com/documentation/SDEN885747/latest/

might be a match to what we've been chasing

Hmm, they did not say explicitly but I'd interpret that as: a store-release can be reordered with a load-acquire,
**if they operate on different atomics**, but that is exactly what macos does with the `LDAPR`, and which does
break things, but since this PR does the release and the acquire on the same atomic, the program order
should still be observed.
So I still think we will need this PR, for formal correctness.
I'm not disagreeing, just looking for cause for why we might have needed this.

I long lost track of all the speculative fixes and newly discovered mishaps in this saga, but it sounded like the cause for you all needing it was ultimately an incorrect understanding about how atomics worked. I mean, there were atomics that saw acquiring loads with no releasing store at all, which does not synchronize.
@nhorman how are your test results?
Both platforms ran all weekend, no failures

Okay, thanks. So since the test had no failures for >96 hours in total now,
my proposal would be to merge this PR first,
then #27012 "Do some cleanup in RCU code"
and keep #27002 on hold, in case there are still test failures reported.
merged to master,3.5,34, and 3.3.  thank you!

review_comments: I think current_idx is not in sync with `lock->reader_idx` is that intentional? I would expect to ue `lock->reader_idx` is here so we will be operating on the same address as ATOMIC_ADD_FETCH() in `get_hold_current_qp()` is referring to. Though I'm not sure it matters.
yes that is the intention `get_hold_current_qp` shall notice that it's `qp_idx` is the wrong one and try the next one.
and yes it matters.  In the case where the race condition can happen this will be the same atomic.
I'm sure I'm missing something. in my opinion we should be doing __ATOMIC_RELEASE on lin 409, because `update_qp()` reads from `&lock->reader_idx` before it modifies `->qp_groups[->reader_idx]`
no that is completely irrelevant, the algorithm would work even if the qp_idx was a random value
